correctness.rationale: For each run \(R\) and shift \(h<p\), the matching sites are exactly an initial interval of length \([R-h]_+\) and a terminal interval of length \([R-(p-h)]_+\). For \(s<t\) the smaller shift dominates the initial intervals and the larger shift dominates terminal intervals; their uncovered gap equals \([R-[R-s]_+-[R-(p-t)]_+]_+\). Summing over all runs is exact. Zero gaps iff \(s+p-t\leq R\) for each run, hence \(s+p-t\leq\min_j r_j\). Counting positive \(s,u\) under \(s+u\leq r\) gives \(\binom r2\), the capped triangular law, and unique minimum-delay pair. Since two host periods cover each residue under shifts \(t<p\), the finite claim follows. Literal independent finite enumeration successfully checked 2,537 tuples, 157,381 shift pairs, 28,563 budgets, and 157,381 finite comparisons. Finite tests are not the proof.

value.rationale: The complete delay-budget spectrum answers a natural two-offset resource-constrained question arising directly from the 2022 definition and its bounded-pseudoperiod decision problem: which subperiod delays suffice, how many under budget, what is the best largest delay, and how many phases fail any rejected pair? The all-alphabet-size, all-positive-run family yields a sharp threshold and nontrivial triangular growth determined solely by the minimum run, plus quantitative exact defects. It goes beyond a single numerical example or an automatic restatement of known upper/lower bounds. The distinct-letter hypothesis is necessary (primitive-period 00101 demonstrates failure without it). No general NP-hardness improvement is claimed.
